newsitem.title: USA: Musicland in technical default of pact.
newsitem.headline: Musicland in technical default of pact.

text.p: Specialty retailer Musicland Stores Corp said Thursday it is in technical default of a financing agreement as a result of a change in accounting and is in talks with its lenders to resolve the issue.
The technical default is not a financial default.

Musicland said the elimination of the company's entire goodwill balance during 1995 and 1996 in accordance with accounting rule FASB 121 results in a technical default of a financing pact on one of the company's real estate properties.
FASB 121 was adopted after this agreement was reached, and a waiver is being discussed with lenders, Musicland said.
In addition, Musicland said it is in technical default of its credit agreement as a result of the reclassification of an operating lease to an owned asset on the company's books.

Musicland said it continues discussions with its revolving credit facility bank group regarding future covenant waivers and its long-term financial outlook. However, the company cautioned that there can be no assurance that needed waivers will be obtained.

Earlier today, Musicland reported 1996 fourth quarter earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization and non-recurring charges of $63.0 million, compared with $66.7 million in the same quarter of 1995.

Including a one-time $40 million restructuring charge for a previously announced program to close unprofitable stores, and a non-recurring $95.3 million non-cash write-down of goodwill to eliminate that intangible asset from its balance sheet, Musicland reported a fourth quarter net loss of $118.6 million.

"Despite a tough year, the company's fourth quarter EBITDA firmed up somewhat relative to the prior year, reflecting the impact of the restructuring efforts and of sales increases in November, December and January," Jack Eugster, chairman, said.

"By aggressively closing stores that lost money in 1996, we are left with a healthier store base, and because the inventory investment recovered from closing these stores exceeded the closing costs, these actions are generating cash," he said in a statement.
"The goodwill write-down reduced 1996 earnings per share by $2.85, but did not reduce cash flow," he noted.

Musicland's sales for the quarter and the year rose 1.8 percent and 5.7 percent, respectively. Sales for the fourth quarter rose to $699.0 million from $686.9 million last year; sales for the full year totaled $1.82 billion versus $1.72 billion in 1995. Comparable-store sales rose 1.2 percent in the fourth quarter and fell 0.6 percent for the full year.

At 1996 year-end, Musicland operated a total of 1,466 stores (87 Media Play stores, 158 On Cue stores, 422 Suncoast stores, 777 Sam Goody/Musicland stores and 22 United Kingdom stores) in 49 states, the United Kingdom, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands.

From January through November 1996, Musicland closed 49 underperforming stores, including 11 Media Play stores. From December 1996 through February 1997, it will have closed 79 additional stores, including 17 Media Play stores. Two more Media Play units will close by the end of the first quarter.

The company said it strictly managed inventory, improving in-stock positions, redeploying inventory dollars, and buying more frequently and closer to sales peaks. Inventory levels at year-end 1996 declined to $506.1 million from $533.7 million at year-end 1995. Musicland also cut costs by streamlining some divisions and closing a Minneapolis distribution center.
